desc:
You are allowed to replace at most one element of nums by any integer value of your choice. Return true if the array can be made non-decreasing this way, meaning nums[i] ≤ nums[i+1] for every valid i. Otherwise return false.

[4, 2, 3]    -> true   (change 4 to 1, or 2 to 4)
[4, 2, 1]    -> false
[3, 4, 2, 3] -> false
hints: If the array has two or more separate places where nums[i] > nums[i+1] that cannot be fixed by one change, the answer is false. Start by finding the first such place.
At a drop nums[i-1] > nums[i] you have two options: lower nums[i-1] or raise nums[i]. Which one is safe depends on nums[i-2].

If nums[i-2] > nums[i] you cannot lower nums[i-1] to nums[i] (it would fall below nums[i-2]), so raise nums[i] to nums[i-1]. Otherwise lower nums[i-1] to nums[i], which keeps the future as small as possible. A second drop after using the change means false.
editorial: Scan from left to right. When you meet a drop nums[i-1] > nums[i], the one allowed change must repair it, and there are only two sensible repairs: set nums[i-1] = nums[i] or set nums[i] = nums[i-1].

Lowering nums[i-1] is only legal when it stays at least nums[i-2], i.e. when i < 2 or nums[i-2] ≤ nums[i]. It is also the better choice, because it leaves the smaller value behind for later comparisons. If that is not legal, raise nums[i] to nums[i-1] (the smallest value that fixes the drop). Count the repairs; a second drop means the answer is false.
The array is modified on a copy while scanning, so later comparisons see the repaired value. Single pass, O(n) time, O(n) for the copy (or O(1) if you restore the value).
